===== https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/archive/exo/ (fetched 2026-10-01)


   MIT Exokernel Operating System

MIT Exokernel Operating System

Putting the Application in Control.
An operating system is interposed between applications and the physical
hardware. Therefore, its structure has a dramatic impact on the performance
and the scope of applications that can be built on it. Since its inception,
the field of operating systems has been attempting to identify an appropriate
structure: previous attempts include the familiar monolithic and micro-kernel
operating systems as well as more exotic language-based and virtual machine
operating systems. Exokernels dramatically depart from this previous work.
An exokernel eliminates the notion that an operating system should provide
abstractions on which applications are built. Instead, it concentrates
solely on securely multiplexing the raw hardware: from basic hardware primitives,
application-level libraries and servers can directly implement traditional
operating system abstractions, specialized for appropriateness and speed.

Structure of an exokernel system. Applications use their
own Library Operating System (LibOS) which

in turn use the exokernel to allocate and deallcate hardware
resources.

We have built several exokernel based systems. The newest exokernel
is XOK, which runs on PC hardware, and ExOS, our first library
operating system (libos). The ExOS library provides a user-level and
extensible implementation of an UNIX operating system. Most UNIX
applications like gcc, perl, apache, tcsh, and telnet compile and work
without changes using ExOS. Further, measurements of application
performance show that ExOS performs at least as well as OpenBSD and
FreeBSD and much better when using specialized libos's. For example,
the Cheetah web server built on top of XOK performs eight times faster
than NCSA or Harvest and three to four times faster than IIS running
on Windows NT Enterprise Edition.   

Check out a [/exo/exo-slides/sld001.htm] slide-show
about exokernels on our [/exo/docs.html] documentation
page.

An alpha-release of our exopc [/exo/distrib.html] distribution 
is currently available. It contains all source and tools required to build
and boot the entire system on a pc. We hope that by making the exopc distribution
publicly available we can interest the 'net community at large in developing
and using exokernels.

For more information on exokernels and related projects see the home
pages of the  [/] Parallel and Distributed
Operating Systems group at the [http://web.mit.edu] MIT
[http://www.lcs.mit.edu] Lab for Computer Science. Papers can
be found at [/PDOS-papers.html] the
PDOS papers page. 

Last updated by Marc 5, 1998.

Dawson Engler

 Dawson Engler 

Hi.

I am a member of Frans Kaashoek's group,
[/] 
Parallel and Distributed Operating Systems.
I spend a lot of my time hacking exokernels and
[http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~engler/pldi96-abstract.html] 
dynamic code generation systems.  I also work 
on the problem of pulling application-level semantics and control
into [magik-abstract.html] compilers.  

My curriculum vitae is available
[cv.ps] 
here. 

I used to have a fetish involving oil, stages, and weights (since
outgrown).  This [jr-calif.html] picture is from the 1991
Jr. California, a "drug-free-for-life" competition, where I finished
2nd.  A reliance on the body's natural supply of androgenic aids
combined with over-exuberant dieting translated into muscles only
slightly larger than those of an olympic marathon runner.  

[cool-people.html] Cool computer-related people and places.

 Some Recent Papers 

 Exokernel Papers 

[sosp-97.ps] 
Application Performance and Flexibility on Exokernel Systems,
  M. Frans Kaashoek, Dawson R. Engler, Gregory R. Ganger,
  H'ector M. Brice~no, Russell Hunt, David Mazi`eres, Thomas Pinckney,
  Robert Grimm, John Jannotti, and Kenneth Mackenzie,
  Proceedings of the Fifteenth ACM Symposium on
  Operating Systems Principles (SOSP).  October, 1997. 

This is the best exokernel paper ever written. It has real application
performance and a cool use of deterministic turing machines that lets
an exokernel trust applications to track what they own without
understanding how they do so.  Slides are available [sosp97-talk.ps] 
here. 

[sosp-95.ps] 
Exokernel: An Operating System Architecture for Application-Level Resource Management,
Dawson R. Engler, M. Frans Kaashoek and James W. O'Toole

This paper appeared in SOSP95 ([exo-sosp-talk.ps]  slides are
available here).  It is the most detailed description of
what an exokernel is and has the most recent numbers.  It is also
rather dense.  A more long-winded version of this paper is available in
the form of [msthesis.ps]  my masters thesis  (though the
material is about 6 months behind that in the SOSP paper).  

[hotos-jeremiad.ps] 
Exterminate All Operating System Abstractions,
Dawson R. Engler and M. Frans Kaashoek

This is a flamy paper describing the philosophical underpinnings of the
exokernel approach.  It appeared in HotOS-V

[serverOS-sigops96.ps] 
Server Operating Systems,
by
[http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~kaashoek/] M. Frans Kaashoek,
[http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~engler/]  Dawson R. Engler,
[http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~ganger/] Gregory R. Ganger,
and [http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~kerr/]  Deborah A. Wallach. 
This paper appears in the 1996 SIGOPS European Workshop,
September 9-11, 1996.

The following position papers give a somewhat dated overview of the 
exokernel project; we are currently implementing a prototype exokernel called
Aegis.

[avm.ps] 
AVM: Application-level Virtual Memory,
Dawson R. Engler, Sandeep Gupta and M. Frans Kaashoek

This paper gives a brief motivation for and description of application-level
virtual memory.  It appeared in HotOS-V

[osdi-exo.ps] 
The Exokernel Approach to Operating System Extensibility,

Dawson R. Engler and M. Frans Kaashoek and James W. O'Toole Jr.

This 1-page precis of the exokernel project appeared in the Proceedings of
First Symposium on Operating System Design and Implementation (OSDI) 

[xsigops.ps] 
The Operating System Kernel as a Secure Programmable Machine, 

Dawson R. Engler and M. Frans Kaashoek and James W. O'Toole Jr.

This is a later version of a position paper that appears in the Proceedings
of the Sixth SIGOPS European Workshop, 1994.  This version appears in
the OSR Special Issue on Extensible Operating Systems.  (The exokernel
philosophy it presents is somewhat out-of-date.)

 Incorporating application semantics and control into compilation 

Magik is a system developed to incorporate application semantics (such
as the meaning of library interfaces and data structures) into the
compiler, thereby allowing it to both optimize and error check them to
the same degree as language constructs.  Magik also allows programmers
to easily add extensions to the compiler.  Since these extensions have
full access to the symbol table, the compiler IR, and data flow
information they can perform operations (such as structure member
profiling) expensive or infeasible by other means.  For an abstract,
click [magik-abstract.html] here; the full paper (which
appeared in the First Conference on Domain-specific Languages) is 
[magik.ps]  here.

The following papers discuss two dynamic code generation systems and a
language designed to support high-level and efficient specification of
dynamically generated code.

 vcode: fast portable dynamic code generation 

[vcode-pldi.ps] 
vcode: a retargetable, extensible, very fast dynamic code generation system, 
by Dawson R. Engler

[http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~engler/pldi96-abstract.html] This paper 
appeared in PLDI '96. Slides are available [vcode-pldi-talk.ps] 
here .  

vcode is a portable system to generate executable code at runtime.  It
generates code in approximately 10 instructions per generated instruction,
and is easily extendable by clients.   A tutorial describing it can be
obtained by clicking [vcode-tutorial.ps]  here.  A beta
version of the system is also [latest-vcode-release.tar.Z]  available.
To get on the vcode mailing list, please email engler@lcs.mit.edu.
[http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~engler/pldi96-abstract.html] Click
here for a bit more information.

 `C: a language for high-level, fast dynamic code generation 

[pldi-tickc.ps] 
`C: A Language for High-Level, Efficient, and Machine-independent
Dynamic Code Generation,
by Dawson R. Engler, Wilson C. Hsieh and M. Frans Kaashoek.
This paper appeared in POPL 1996.  Slides are available 
[tickc-popl-talk.ps]  here. 

[tickc-pldi-submit.ps] 
tcc: A System for Fast, Flexible, and High-level Dynamic Code Generation
by Massimiliano Poletto, Dawson R. Engler and M. Frans Kaashoek.
This paper will appear in PLDI 1997. A preliminary release of the tcc
compiler can be obtained from 
[http:/tickc] the tickc homepage.

[wcsss.ps] 
tcc: A Template-Based Compiler for `C
by Massimiliano Poletto, Dawson R. Engler and M. Frans Kaashoek.
This paper appeared in WCSSS 1996.  A preliminary release of the tcc
compiler can be obtained from
[http:/tickc] the tickc homepage.

 DCG 

[dcg.ps] 
DCG: An Efficient, Retargetable Dynamic Code Generator, 

by Dawson R. Engler and Todd A. Proebsting.
This paper appeared in ASPLOS 94 ([dcg-asplos-talk.ps] 
click here for slides). The system it describes
has been superseded by [pldi96-abstract.html]  vcode.

The following three papers discuss a network
system built on top of the exokernel.

[sigcomm96.ps] 
ASHs:  Application-specific handlers for high-performance messaging,
by
[http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~kerr/] 
Deborah A. Wallach,
[http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~engler/] 
Dawson R. Engler,
and [http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~kaashoek/] 
M. Frans Kaashoek. 

The paper appeared in 
[http://www.acm.org/sigcomm/sigcomm96/index.html] 
ACM Communication Architectures, Protocols, and Applications (SIGCOMM '96).
Portions of its implementation are more thoroughly explored in:

[ash-osdi.ps] 
Design and Implementation of a Modular, Flexible, and Fast System for
Dynamic Protocol Composition,
by
[http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~engler/] 
Dawson R. Engler,
[http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~kerr/] 
Deborah A. Wallach,
and [http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~kaashoek/] 
M. Frans Kaashoek.  

[dpf-sigcomm96.ps] 
DPF: Fast, Flexible Message Demultiplexing using Dynamic Code Generation,
by
[http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~engler/] 
Dawson R. Engler
and [http://www.pdos.lcs.mit.edu/~kaashoek/] 
M. Frans Kaashoek. 

The paper appeared in 
[http://www.acm.org/sigcomm/sigcomm96/index.html] 
ACM Communication Architectures, Protocols, and Applications (SIGCOMM '96). 
Slides from the talk are available [dpf-talk.ps]  here. 
A beta release of the system is available [dpf.tar.gz]  here.
DPF is described more fully 
[dpf.html]  here.

The following two papers were written when I was at University of Arizona

by Dawson R. Engler.

[fine-grain-93.ps] 
Filaments: Efficient Support for Fine-Grain Parallelism, 
by Dawson R. Engler, Gregory R. Andrews, and David K. Lowenthal.
